title: Syllabus
text:
Instructor
Course




 John Paul Helveston
 Thursdays


 Tompkins 201
 Aug. 26 - Dec. 7, 2027


 jph@gwu.edu
 3:30PM - 6:00PM EST






The bottleneck on what you can build is no longer what you already know — it’s your workflow discipline and your ability to direct an agent. This course teaches you to use AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex to build ambitious things you don’t yet know how to build, while developing the professional engineering habits — version control with Git and GitHub, testing, continuous integration with GitHub Actions, and deployment with GitHub Pages — that make agentic work sustainable and trustworthy. The course runs in two parts. In Part 1: Working with an agent, we start with Git by hand, look under the hood at how large language models work (and fail), and then climb from high-touch collaboration with an agent toward delegating work and automatically verifying it. In Part 2: Building with LLMs, we apply the workflow to real data analysis in Python (polars, plotnine, and Great Tables), call LLMs from your own code with chatlas, connect agents to tools with the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and orchestrate multiple agents. Each week pairs a hands-on workflow concept taught live in class with an ambitious take-home build — a deployed personal website, a novel in an author’s voice, a video game, a cloud robot, an AI-powered tool, and more — and a short reading that connects the work to the bigger picture. A team project runs alongside, with in-class studio time for collaboration. By the end, you’ll have transferable engineering workflow skills, the ability to work with code and data through an agent, the judgment to know when to trust (and when to verify) AI output, and — most importantly — the ability to teach yourself new domains so you can tackle harder problems in the future.



Students must have completed at least one programming course (e.g., CSCI 1012 or equivalent) or have comparable experience working in at least one programming language. Most of our code will be in Python, but you do not need to be a Python expert. You should be comfortable reading code, following the logic of a program, and recognizing when something is wrong — these are the skills that let you supervise an agent rather than blindly trust it. Students with zero coding experience will find this course very difficult.

title: Syllabus
text:
Participation & Attendance
Attendance will be taken and is the primary driver of your participation grade.
In-class work is hands-on and ungraded — but it is practice for the build you do at home. The take-home builds assume the skills we develop together in class, so missing class costs you twice: once on participation, and again on a much harder homework. Plan to attend in person every week.

title: Syllabus
text:
Individual Builds
There are 11 builds, each an ambitious project in a domain you likely haven’t worked in before. Each build is delivered as a GitHub repository that includes the full conversation history with the agent, plus a short reflection on the build’s assigned reading. Grading focuses on prompt quality, evidence of iterative collaboration, final product quality, and thoughtful use of the week’s workflow skill. Builds are graded with a checklist, you may resubmit once for a revised score, and your lowest build score is dropped.

title: Syllabus
text:
Oral Code Walkthroughs
Twice during the semester you’ll spend 5–10 minutes in class walking the instructor through one of your builds: how it works, and why you (or the agent) did it that way. The goal is durable learning. If you can’t explain what the agent built, you don’t yet own it.

title: Syllabus
text:
Team Project
Throughout the semester you’ll work in teams of 3–4 on an open-ended project of your own design — the one piece of fully open-ended work in the course. It is broken into milestone deliverables (proposal, interim report, final report, presentation). See the project overview for details.

title: Syllabus
text:
AI Tools and Cost
You’ll need an AI coding agent for this course, and the most economical option is a subscription of about $20/month:

Claude Pro (for Claude Code), or
ChatGPT Plus (for Codex).

Choose one. You’re welcome to use a different agentic coding tool instead (e.g., Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode), since the underlying skills transfer, but in-class instruction will use Claude Code and Codex.
Why a subscription and not the API? Agentic coding burns a lot of tokens. Paying per token through an API would cost far more than a flat monthly subscription. We recommend a subscription for exactly that reason. I recognize that $20/month is a real cost. We are pursuing institutional access, so check Slack before you pay, and let me know if the cost is a barrier.
API access for Meetings 10–11. A subscription does not include API access, and we’ll call LLMs from Python code with chatlas in those meetings. You can do this at no cost with a free-tier or local model, or by loading about $5 of credit on a provider’s API and using a small model. The course materials work with any provider. We’ll go over the options in class before Meeting 10.

title: Syllabus
text:
Generative-AI Use Policy
Using AI agents is not “cheating” in this course — it is the core skill being taught. Using the language of the MIT report on AI and education, the policy for individual builds is required use of generative AI: you must use an agentic coding tool and submit your full conversation history. You remain fully responsible for the correctness, quality, and originality of everything you submit: read what the agent produces, run it, and fix it when it’s wrong.
There are two AI-free exceptions, each with a reason:

Meeting 1 and Build 1 (Git by hand). You can’t supervise an agent that uses Git until you can use Git yourself.
Reading reflections. These are written in your own words, because the point is your own thinking about the reading.

Other course commitments:

No AI detectors. We do not use AI-detection software, which is unreliable. The evidence of your process is your conversation logs and your Git history.
Instructor disclosure. I use AI in preparing course materials and in drafting grading feedback, and I review everything before you see it.
Log privacy. Conversation logs are seen only by the course staff and used only for grading. Remove API keys, passwords, and personal data from your logs before you submit them.
Responsible use. We’ll discuss failure modes, ethics, environmental cost, and when not to use AI throughout the course.

Detailed disclosure requirements appear in each assignment.

title: Team Project Overview
text:
The team project is the capstone of the course — and the only piece of fully open-ended work. In teams of 3–4, you’ll propose and build an ambitious, real-world project of your own design, applying every workflow skill from the semester: version control, planning, skills, verification, continuous integration, deployment, LLM APIs, MCP, and (where it helps) multi-agent orchestration.
Teams form in Meeting 5. From Meeting 9 on, the last ~45 minutes of each class is team studio time, where the instructor checks in with each team. The final two meetings are dedicated studio sessions, and we learn collaboration workflows (pull request reviews, issues, and parallel agents in git worktrees) live in Meeting 12.

Learning Objectives:
Having successfully completed this course, students will be able to:

Explain how large language models work and why they fail (hallucination, sycophancy, limited context).
Direct an AI agent to build real products in domains they haven’t learned before.
Use Git, GitHub, and pull requests fluently as everyday version control and collaboration tools.
Verify agent-built systems with tests, review agents, and continuous integration with GitHub Actions, and deploy to the web with GitHub Pages.
Analyze data with an agent using Python, and check the numbers, not just the plots.
Call LLMs from their own code, and connect agents to tools using the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Orchestrate multiple agents and collaborate with teammates on a shared codebase.
Use AI responsibly: verify outputs, disclose AI use, and protect secrets and personal data.
Teach themselves a new domain using an agent — the meta-skill that outlasts any single tool.

Most of our code will be in Python, but you do not need to be a Python expert. Quarto and Python
Quarto renders .qmd files containing Python code using its Jupyter engine. You won’t ever open or create a notebook, but the project’s uv environment needs ipykernel installed, and Quarto has to use that environment. The simplest way is to run Quarto through uv:
uv add ipykernel
uv run quarto render report.qmd

title: Software & Setup
section: Choose and install an AI coding agent
text:
Choose and install an AI coding agent
We will use agentic coding tools all semester, so you need one. Instruction will use Claude Code and Codex, and the underlying skills transfer between them.

Step 1: Get a subscription (about $20/month)

Claude Code requires at least a Claude Pro subscription. A free account isn’t enough.
Codex requires a paid ChatGPT plan (Plus is fine).

We recommend a subscription rather than API billing because agentic coding uses so many tokens that per-token API costs would be far higher. Check Slack for whether the class has an institutional arrangement before paying for your own.


Step 2: Install your agent
Follow the official instructions: the Claude Code quickstart or the Codex repository. If you get stuck, we’ll sort it out together before or after the first class.


Other agents
You’re welcome to use another agent (Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode…). In-class instruction will use Claude Code and Codex, so you may need to translate tool-specific steps yourself.


Claude Code ↔︎ Codex
Both tools read the same open standards, so most of what we build works in either:

API access for chatlas (Meetings 10–11)
A Claude or ChatGPT subscription does not include API access. For the chatlas meetings you have three options, and the code is the same for all of them (you change one line to switch providers):

Free: the Gemini API free tier (via chatlas’s ChatGoogle).
Free: a local model through Ollama (via ChatOllama).
About $5: load credit with a provider and use a small, cheap model.

We’ll cover how to set this up, and how to keep API keys out of your code and out of your Git history, in class before Meeting 10.
